names.name: Atayal ptasan
names.said: Forehead for both; a man's chin when he fathers a child; a woman's cheeks when she can weave

when.label: Banned by the Japanese administration in 1930

practice.suppressed_by: banned by the Japanese colonial administration in 1930, for its link to headhunting
practice.note: A qualification, not an ornament: the face says the skill has been demonstrated.

text.what: Taiwan: a band down the forehead, and a second mark earned — by a man for taking a head, by a woman for mastering the loom.
text.story:
The rule was a gate. No face marks, no marriage; no face marks, no crossing to the ancestors at death. A girl learned to weave at ten or twelve and had to master it before her cheeks were marked, which makes the tattoo a certificate of competence held on the most visible surface a person has.

Japan banned it in 1930. Christianity finished the job. The marks are now on elderly faces and on the museum wall.
